newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Lebed urges "dictatorship of law".
newsitem.headline: Russia's Lebed urges "dictatorship of law".

text.p: Former general Alexander Lebed, his sights set firmly on the Russian presidency, was quoted on Thursday as saying he sought to create a "dictatorship of law" but would never sanction a return to brutality and labour camps.
Lebed, in an interview with Obshchaya Gazeta newspaper, acknowledged that by background he was a man of war.
"I was trained to rip off heads and I can do this superbly. I can be professionally cruel," he said. But these instincts would not serve him as a politician.
"If I was not born with a built-in kind smile on my face, that does not mean at all that I am a tyrant," he said, mocking his notorious grim look, black humour and basso profundo voice.
"I can say...that I will not do anything illegitimate, anything cruel," he added. "No camps, no GULAG's. We have seen this and this system proved a complete failure."

Lebed, 46, a former paratrooper, fell out with President Boris Yeltsin after helping him to election victory in July. He was sacked after a brief spell as national security chief in the Kremlin, but not before forging a deal to end war in Chechnya.
He left with few good impressions of Yeltsin's entourage.
"They are like spiders in a can," Lebed said. "They feel that they are not there for long. Their aim is to grab as much as they can in the shortest time."
Lebed said he believed that Yeltsin, who underwent heart surgery in November and suffered pneumonia in January, was too weak to rule Russia.
"(His condition) is really bad," Lebed said. "It's an open secret that they (Yeltsin's entourage) have written him off."

In a clear contrast to what he sees as the decline of other Kremlin leaders, Lebed presented himself as a mentally and physically sound person keen on the simple joys typical of many Russians but not given to their vices.
"I have no hobby," he said. "I hate hunting and I am no fisher. I cannot play tennis and...have no desire to learn to play. I like mushroom hunting and skiing. I also like to play chess."
"I have not drunk for three years," he added. "I woke up on Dec 25, 1993, and decided to try and become the most sober person in this country. Now I am thinking about quitting smoking."
Lebed, considered the most likely winner if presidential elections were held now, shrugged off personal attacks from both communist and liberal opponents.
"Personality doesn't matter. What matters is a dictatorship of law," he said "It should be a fool-proof system."
Lebed made clear that he saw his main aim as creating a powerful middle class in Russia, which he sees as guarantor of stability and an effective market economy in the country.
But he appeared sceptical about liberal rulers in Russia as well as in other former Soviet republics.

"It was the liberal (Mircea) Snegur who started war in the Dnestr region, it was the liberal Yeltsin who started war in Russia," he said referring to Moldova's former president's drive in 1992 to subdue the breakaway Dnestr region and a campaign launched by Yeltsin to crush rebel Chechnya in 1994.
"I stopped both wars," Lebed said.
"Now tell me, who is more of a liberal?"
